questions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript, and how does it behave differently for var, function declarations, and function expressions?
questions.answer: Hoisting describes how the JS engine processes declarations during parsing, before executing code line by line, so declarations appear usable earlier in a scope than where they are written. It behaves differently per declaration type. Function declarations (function foo(){}) are fully hoisted - both the name and the body - so they can be called before their line in the source. var declarations are hoisted and auto-initialized to undefined; only the declaration moves up, not the assignment, so reading a var before its assignment line gives undefined instead of an error. let, const, and class declarations are hoisted in the sense that the engine reserves the binding for the whole scope, but they stay uninitialized and inaccessible until their declaration line runs (the temporal dead zone) - accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError. Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to a variable only hoist the variable itself, not the function value, so calling them before the assignment line throws (a TypeError if declared with var, since it's undefined at that point; a ReferenceError if declared with let/const, due to the TDZ).

questions.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
questions.answer: === (strict equality) compares both type and value with no conversion: operands of different types are always considered unequal. == (loose/abstract equality) first coerces operands to a common type using a defined algorithm before comparing - e.g., a number vs. a string converts the string to a number, and null is loosely equal only to undefined and nothing else. This is why '5' == 5 is true but '5' === 5 is false, and why [] == false is true (the array coerces to '' then to 0, and false coerces to 0). Because the coercion rules have surprising edge cases, common guidance (also reflected in linters like ESLint's eqeqeq rule) is to default to === and reserve == for the one common intentional idiom, value == null, which matches both null and undefined in a single check.

questions.question: What are JavaScript's "falsy" values, and how does truthy/falsy evaluation affect conditionals?
questions.answer: JavaScript coerces any value to a boolean in conditional contexts (if, while, ternary, &&, ||, !!). There are exactly eight falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n (BigInt zero), '' (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else is truthy - importantly including [] and {}, which trips people up because they look 'empty' but are still object references, hence truthy. This matters practically for guard checks: if (arr.length) is safer than if (arr) when you actually want to test 'the array has items,' since a non-empty array reference is always truthy regardless of its contents.

questions.question: Why does typeof null return "object"?
questions.answer: typeof null returns 'object', which is a well-known historical bug rather than a deliberate design choice. In the original 1995 JavaScript engine, values were represented as a type tag plus a value, and objects had the type tag 0; null was represented internally as the null pointer, which happened to also carry a type tag of 0, so it was misidentified as an object by the typeof check. By the time this was widely recognized, enough code on the web depended on the existing behavior that fixing it was considered too risky - a TC39 proposal to correct it was ultimately rejected for backward-compatibility reasons. In practice this means typeof x === 'object' cannot be used to exclude null; you need an explicit x === null check alongside it.

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
questions.answer: Both represent 'no value,' but with different intent and origin. undefined is what JavaScript assigns automatically: a declared-but-unassigned variable, a missing function argument, a missing object property, or a function with no return statement all evaluate to undefined - the language's default 'nothing here yet.' null is a value a developer assigns deliberately to represent an intentionally empty or absent reference. They are loosely equal (null == undefined is true) but not strictly equal (null === undefined is false), and typeof null is 'object' while typeof undefined is 'undefined'. A common convention: let undefined mean 'not set,' and use null when explicitly signaling the deliberate absence of a value that was expected to exist (e.g., a lookup function returning null for 'not found').

questions.question: What is NaN, and how do you correctly check whether a value is NaN (including the difference between isNaN() and Number.isNaN())?
questions.answer: NaN is a special numeric value meaning 'not a number,' produced by invalid math operations such as 0/0 or Number('abc'). Its defining oddity is that NaN !== NaN - per the IEEE 754 floating-point spec, it's the only value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself. The global isNaN(x) first coerces x to a number and then checks whether the result is NaN, so isNaN('hello') is true (because 'hello' coerces to NaN) even though 'hello' obviously isn't the NaN value - this coercion makes isNaN() unreliable as a strict check. Number.isNaN(x) does no coercion and only returns true if x is literally the NaN value, so Number.isNaN('hello') correctly returns false. The reliable way to check for NaN specifically is Number.isNaN(x), or the coercion-free Object.is(x, NaN).

questions.question: How does JavaScript's implicit type coercion work? (e.g., what do 1 + "2" and 1 - "2" evaluate to, and why?)
questions.answer: JavaScript performs implicit type coercion whenever an operator receives operands of mismatched types, following operator-specific rules. The + operator is overloaded for both numeric addition and string concatenation: if either operand is (or coerces to) a string, + concatenates, so 1 + '2' becomes '1' + '2', which is '12'. Every other arithmetic operator (-, *, /, %) only has a numeric meaning, so JavaScript coerces both operands to numbers first: 1 - '2' converts '2' to the number 2, giving -1. This asymmetry - + being 'special' while every other arithmetic operator forces numeric conversion - is one of the most common gotcha questions. Similar coercion also drives == comparisons (via the Abstract Equality algorithm's type-conversion steps) and boolean contexts (via the internal ToBoolean rules behind truthy/falsy evaluation).

questions.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? Under what circumstances?
questions.answer: Yes. Because a closure keeps a live reference to variables in its enclosing scope, any large object captured by a long-lived closure - one attached to a persistent event listener, an interval timer that's never cleared, or stored in a growing cache - is kept reachable, and therefore kept in memory, for as long as that closure exists, even if nothing else in the program still needs it. Common leak patterns: attaching event listeners inside a closure and never removing them when the related element is destroyed, setInterval callbacks that close over large data and are never cleared with clearInterval, and accumulating closures in an array or cache without ever pruning old entries. The fix is generally lifecycle discipline - removing listeners, clearing timers, and releasing references you no longer need - or, for cache-like use cases, using a WeakMap/WeakSet so entries can be garbage-collected automatically once nothing else references the key.

questions.question: How is the value of this determined in JavaScript, and how does it differ between regular functions and arrow functions?
What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
questions.answer: All three let you explicitly set what this refers to inside a function, but they differ in when the function runs and how arguments are passed. fn.call(thisArg, a, b, c) invokes fn immediately with this set to thisArg, passing arguments individually. fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b, c]) invokes fn immediately as well, but takes arguments as a single array - useful when arguments already exist in array form, or for method-borrowing tricks like Math.max.apply(null, arr). fn.bind(thisArg, a, b) does not call fn - it returns a new function with this permanently bound to thisArg (and optionally some leading arguments pre-filled/partially applied), to be invoked later; that returned function's this cannot be overridden again, even by another bind or by call/apply. A common real use is binding a class method in the constructor (this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)) so it keeps the right this when detached and passed as a callback or event handler.

questions.question: Beyond this binding, what are the practical differences between arrow functions and regular functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions differ from regular functions in several concrete ways beyond this binding. They have no own arguments object - they inherit arguments from the enclosing scope, or throw a ReferenceError if there is none. They cannot be used as constructors - calling one with new throws a TypeError, since arrow functions have no internal [[Construct]] and no prototype property (arrowFn.prototype is undefined). They cannot be generator functions - there is no arrow-function equivalent of function*. They support implicit return for a single-expression body (x => x * 2), whereas regular functions always require an explicit return. And because their this is lexically fixed at definition, call/apply/bind on an arrow function can only pass arguments, never rebind this. Practically, arrow functions suit short callbacks and preserving this inside class methods or nested functions, but are a poor fit for object methods needing a dynamic this, or for anything meant to be called with new.

questions.question: What is an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression), and why would you use one?
questions.answer: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression is a function that is defined and executed in a single step, typically written as (function () { ... })(); or with an arrow function (() => { ... })();. Wrapping the function in parentheses forces the parser to treat it as an expression rather than a declaration, which is required for it to be invoked immediately in this way. Before block-scoped let/const and ES modules existed, IIFEs were the primary way to create a private scope, avoiding global-namespace pollution and implementing the module pattern by returning only a public API while keeping implementation details closed over privately. They're also used to run setup code exactly once, and historically to capture a variable's per-iteration value in a loop when only var was available. Block scope and ES modules now cover many of the original use cases, but IIFEs still appear in bundler output and quick, isolated scoping tricks.

questions.question: What is currying in JavaScript, and how would you implement a curry function?
questions.answer:
Currying transforms a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument (or subset), returning a new function until all arguments have arrived and the original function can finally run. It's a functional-programming technique for creating specialized, partially-applied functions from a general one.

const curry = (fn) => (...args) =>
 args.length >= fn.length
 ? fn(...args)
 : (...more) => curry(fn)(...args, ...more);

const add3 = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
const curried = curry(add3);
curried(1)(2)(3); // 6
curried(1, 2)(3); // 6
curried(1)(2, 3); // 6

A practical use case is building reusable, specialized functions - e.g., deriving const double = multiply(2) from a generic multiply(a, b) - or pre-filling common configuration for a logger or API-request function and passing around a narrower function. This implementation uses fn.length (the function's declared arity) to know when enough arguments have been collected.

questions.question: What is a higher-order function? Give examples using JavaScript's built-in array methods.
questions.answer: A higher-order function either accepts one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both - treating functions as first-class values like any other data. JavaScript's built-in array methods are the most common everyday example: map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach(), and sort() all take a callback and use it to transform, filter, or compare elements. Functions like debounce, throttle, curry, and once are higher-order because they take a function and return a new, wrapped function; compose/pipe utilities that combine several functions into one are another classic case. Higher-order functions are foundational to functional-style JavaScript: they factor out what varies (the callback logic) from what stays the same (the iteration or wrapping mechanism), producing more reusable and composable code than manually written loops.

questions.question: What is prototypal inheritance, and how does it differ from classical (class-based) inheritance?
questions.answer: In classical (class-based) inheritance, as in Java or C++, classes are blueprints and objects are concrete instances created from a class; inheritance means one class formally extends another. JavaScript's model is different: every object has an internal link to another object, its prototype, and objects can inherit directly from other objects - there is no separate class construct underneath (the ES6 class keyword is syntactic sugar over this same mechanism, not a new inheritance model). When a property lookup misses on an object, the engine walks up the chain of prototypes until it finds the property or reaches null. This is more accurately described as delegation than inheritance: an object doesn't copy its prototype's properties, it defers to them at lookup time, so changes to a prototype are visible to every object that delegates to it, even after those objects were created - something classical inheritance doesn't allow. MDN notes the prototypal model is, in fact, more flexible than the classical one, though it can feel unfamiliar to developers coming from class-based languages.

questions.question: What is the difference between creating an object with a constructor function, Object.create(), and the ES6 class syntax?
questions.answer: All three create objects that share behavior via the prototype chain, but with different ergonomics. A constructor function is a regular function invoked with new, which creates a new object, sets its prototype to ConstructorFn.prototype, binds this to it, and returns it implicitly; shared methods are added manually onto ConstructorFn.prototype. Object.create(proto) creates a new object with its prototype set directly to proto, with no constructor function or new involved - useful for precise control of the prototype chain, including Object.create(null) for an object with no inherited properties at all, not even toString. class syntax (ES6) is sugar over the same constructor-function-plus-prototype mechanism - a class still produces a function under the hood, and methods still end up on ClassName.prototype - but adds cleaner syntax for constructors, inheritance (extends/super), getters/setters, and stricter behavior (classes aren't hoisted the same way, and calling one without new throws). Modern codebases generally prefer class for readability, reserving Object.create() for cases needing direct prototype manipulation; using Object.create() to build multi-level inheritance chains is no longer the recommended pattern for that specifically.

questions.question: How does the ES6 class keyword relate to JavaScript's underlying prototype-based model?
questions.answer: JavaScript remains prototype-based even after ES6 introduced class - class doesn't add a new inheritance model, it's syntax that compiles to the same constructor-function-plus-prototype-chain mechanism that existed before. class Foo { method() {} } still produces a function Foo, and method still lives on Foo.prototype, exactly as if written manually as Foo.prototype.method = function () {}. class Bar extends Foo links Bar.prototype's internal prototype to Foo.prototype (so instance methods are inherited via the chain) and separately links Bar itself to Foo (so static members are inherited too) - the same relationship Object.setPrototypeOf could establish manually. What class syntax adds are guardrails: class bodies run in strict mode automatically, class declarations are subject to the temporal dead zone rather than being hoisted like function declarations, calling a class without new throws a TypeError, and super gives clean access to a parent's constructor and methods. So classes are syntactic sugar, but understanding the prototype chain underneath remains essential for reasoning about method lookup, instanceof, and performance.

questions.question: What is the JavaScript event loop, and how do the call stack, Web APIs, and the task/callback queue interact?
questions.answer: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so the event loop is the mechanism that lets it handle asynchronous work (timers, network responses, DOM events) without blocking. The call stack executes synchronous code one frame at a time. When code calls an async Web/Node API (setTimeout, fetch, a DOM event listener), that work is handed off to the browser or Node runtime, which performs it outside the JS thread and, once complete, places the corresponding callback into a queue rather than running it immediately. The event loop's job is strict but simple: continuously check whether the call stack is empty, and if so, take the next callback from a queue and push it onto the stack to run. This is why setTimeout(fn, 0) never runs immediately - fn can only run once the currently executing synchronous code finishes and the stack is clear, even with a zero-millisecond delay.

questions.question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks (e.g., Promise callbacks vs. setTimeout)?
questions.answer: Beyond the macrotask (or 'task') queue - used by setTimeout, setInterval, UI events, and I/O callbacks, of which one is processed per full loop iteration - there's a separate, higher-priority microtask queue used by Promise .then/.catch/.finally callbacks, queueMicrotask(), and MutationObserver notifications. The rule: whenever the call stack becomes empty, the engine fully drains the microtask queue - running every microtask, including any new ones enqueued while draining - before it takes even one more task off the macrotask queue or lets the browser render. This is why Promise callbacks consistently run before a setTimeout(fn, 0) callback scheduled earlier in the same tick: Promise.resolve().then(...) is a microtask and jumps ahead of any pending macrotasks once synchronous code finishes. A practical implication: because microtasks fully drain before the next macrotask, a microtask that keeps enqueuing more microtasks can starve the event loop and block rendering or timers indefinitely.

questions.question: What problem do Promises solve compared to plain callbacks, and what is "callback hell"?
questions.answer: Before Promises, asynchronous operations were composed by passing a callback to run on completion. Chaining several dependent async steps this way - each nested inside the previous callback - produces deeply indented, hard-to-read code informally called 'callback hell' or the 'pyramid of doom,' and it makes error handling awkward because every callback needs its own error-first check, with no unified way to propagate a failure up the chain. Promises represent 'a value that will exist in the future' as a first-class object with a defined state machine (pending, then fulfilled or rejected), letting async steps chain with .then() calls that flatten into a linear sequence instead of nested callbacks, and letting errors from any step be caught in one place with .catch() rather than needing per-step handling. async/await builds further on Promises to let asynchronous code be written and read like synchronous code, using ordinary try/catch for error handling.

questions.question: What are the three states of a Promise, and how do .then(), .catch(), and .finally() work?
questions.answer: A Promise has exactly three states: pending (initial, neither fulfilled nor rejected), fulfilled (the operation succeeded, with a resulting value), and rejected (the operation failed, with a reason). Once a Promise settles (fulfills or rejects), that outcome is permanent and cannot change again. .then(onFulfilled, onRejected) registers callbacks for the fulfilled and, optionally, rejected cases and returns a new Promise, which is what enables chaining - each .then() can return a plain value (auto-wrapped into a resolved Promise) or another Promise (which the chain waits on). .catch(onRejected) is shorthand for .then(undefined, onRejected), conventionally placed at the end of a chain to handle a rejection from any earlier step. .finally(onFinally) runs a callback regardless of whether the Promise fulfilled or rejected, without receiving the value or reason - useful for cleanup like hiding a loading spinner - and it passes the original settlement through unchanged unless its own callback throws.

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(), Promise.race(), and Promise.any()?
questions.answer: All four take an iterable of Promises and return a single new Promise, but settle under different conditions. Promise.all() fulfills with an array of all values, in input order, once every input Promise fulfills, and rejects immediately with the first rejection reason as soon as any input rejects ('fail fast') - best when every operation must succeed. Promise.allSettled() always fulfills once every input has settled one way or another, returning an array of {status: 'fulfilled', value} or {status: 'rejected', reason} objects - best when you need the outcome of every operation, successes and failures alike. Promise.race() settles as soon as the first input Promise settles, adopting whichever value or rejection comes first - useful for timeouts, racing a real request against a setTimeout-based rejection. Promise.any() fulfills with the first input Promise to fulfill, ignoring rejections, and only rejects (with an AggregateError collecting every reason) if all inputs reject - useful when you want the fastest successful result and don't care which source produced it.

questions.question: How does async/await work under the hood, and how does it relate to Promises?
questions.answer: async/await is syntax built on top of Promises, not a separate concurrency mechanism. Declaring a function async guarantees it always returns a Promise - a returned plain value is automatically wrapped in a resolved Promise, and a thrown error produces a rejected Promise. Inside an async function, await expr pauses that function's execution (without blocking the rest of the program) until the Promise expr settles: if it fulfills, await evaluates to the fulfillment value; if it rejects, await throws that rejection, catchable with an ordinary try/catch. Under the hood, each await is effectively a .then() continuation - the code after await is scheduled to resume as a microtask once the awaited Promise settles - so 'it looks synchronous but actually schedules continuations through the microtask queue' is an accurate mental model. This is why code before the first await in an async function still runs synchronously, while code after await never runs in the same synchronous tick as the call that invoked the function.

questions.question: How do you handle errors in async/await code, and how does that differ from error handling in a .then()/.catch() chain?
questions.answer: In a .then() chain, errors are handled with .catch() (or the second argument to .then), typically placed once at the end to catch a rejection from any earlier step - a single centralized handler, but easy to forget, which silently swallows errors if omitted. With async/await, since a rejected awaited Promise throws inside the function, the awaited calls can be wrapped in an ordinary try { ... } catch (err) { ... } block, just like synchronous error handling, which many find more readable and which composes naturally with a finally block for cleanup. A shared gotcha either way: an error thrown inside a .then() callback (or after an await) that isn't caught anywhere produces an 'unhandled promise rejection,' which modern browsers and Node log as a warning (and which some Node configurations treat as fatal) - so every async chain should end in a .catch() or be wrapped in try/catch if it's awaited.

questions.question: What are the differences between map(), filter(), and reduce()? Could you implement a simplified polyfill for one?
What is the difference between forEach() and map()?
questions.answer: Both iterate every array element with a callback, but forEach() always returns undefined and is used purely for side effects (logging, mutating something external), while map() returns a brand-new array built from the callback's return values and is meant for transformation - its result should generally be used. A common code smell interviewers watch for is array.forEach(x => result.push(transform(x))), where array.map(transform) would be clearer and avoids manually managing an external accumulator. Neither method can be stopped early (no break equivalent); a plain for loop, for...of with break, or some()/every() (which do support early exit) are better fits when early termination is needed.

questions.question: How do destructuring assignment and default values work for arrays and objects?
questions.answer:
Destructuring assignment unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables in one expression. Array destructuring is positional: const [a, b] = [1, 2]. Object destructuring is by property name: const {x, y} = point, and can rename while unpacking: const {x: posX} = point. Both support default values, which apply only when the corresponding value is undefined (not for other falsy values like null or 0):

const [a = 10, b = 20] = [5]; // a = 5, b = 20
const { count = 0 } = {}; // count = 0

Destructuring also supports nested patterns (const {a: {b}} = obj), skipping array elements (const [, second] = arr), and combining with rest (const [first, ...rest] = arr). It's heavily used in function parameters (function greet({ name, greeting = 'Hello' }) {}) to provide named, defaulted options without a separate options object.

questions.question: What is the spread operator, and how does it differ from rest parameters?
questions.answer: Both use ... syntax but in opposite directions. Spread expands an iterable (array, string, Set, etc.) or an object's own enumerable properties into individual elements or properties, used in array/object literals and function calls: [...arr1, ...arr2] merges arrays, {...obj1, ...obj2} shallow-merges objects (later keys win on conflict), and Math.max(...numbers) spreads an array into individual arguments. Rest does the opposite - it collects multiple remaining items into a single array or object, used in destructuring and function parameter lists: function sum(...nums) {} gathers all arguments into an array nums, and const [first, ...rest] = arr collects everything after the first element. A rest parameter must be the last parameter in a function's parameter list, or the last element in a destructuring pattern - anything after it is a syntax error.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy of an object, and what are common ways to create each?
questions.answer: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level of an object or array - primitive values are copied by value, but any nested object or array is copied by reference, so mutating a nested structure in the copy still affects the original, and vice versa. Common ways to shallow-copy: the spread operator ({...obj}, [...arr]), Object.assign({}, obj), and Array.prototype.slice()/concat() for arrays. A deep copy recursively duplicates every level, making nested objects fully independent between original and copy. Common ways to deep-copy: structuredClone(obj) (the modern built-in, which supports circular references, Map, Set, and Date), JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) (simple but loses functions, undefined values, Symbol keys, converts Date objects to strings, and breaks on circular references), or a library like Lodash's cloneDeep. Choosing shallow vs. deep depends on whether the data has nested mutable structures that need to be isolated - shallow copies are cheaper and sufficient for flat data.

questions.question: What do Object.freeze(), Object.seal(), and Object.preventExtensions() each do, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: All three progressively restrict how much an object can change, from least to most restrictive. Object.preventExtensions(obj) blocks adding new properties, but existing properties can still be modified or deleted, and their descriptors are untouched. Object.seal(obj) does everything preventExtensions does, plus marks all existing properties as non-configurable - so they can't be deleted and their enumerability/configurability can't change - but values of existing writable properties can still be reassigned. Object.freeze(obj) is the strictest: it does everything seal does, plus makes all existing data properties non-writable, so their values can't be reassigned either. The result is a shallow-immutable object: attempts to add, remove, or change top-level properties silently fail in sloppy mode or throw a TypeError in strict mode. Crucially, Object.freeze() is shallow - nested objects inside a frozen object are not themselves frozen and remain fully mutable, which surprises people expecting deep immutability; a recursive deep-freeze helper is needed to freeze nested structures.

questions.question: What is optional chaining (?.) and the nullish coalescing operator (??), and how do they differ from &&/||-based patterns?
questions.answer: Optional chaining (?.) safely accesses a property, calls a method, or indexes into an array without a preceding null/undefined check crashing the code - if the value immediately before ?. is null or undefined, the whole expression short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing: user?.address?.city, obj.method?.(), arr?.[0]. Nullish coalescing (??) provides a default value, but only when the left side is null or undefined - unlike ||, which falls back on any falsy value: count ?? 10 keeps count if it's 0 or '', whereas count || 10 would incorrectly replace a legitimate 0 with 10. This distinction is the main reason ?? was introduced, and it's a frequent gotcha: 0 || 'default' gives 'default', but 0 ?? 'default' gives 0. Note that ?? cannot be mixed directly with && or || without parentheses - a || b ?? c is a SyntaxError.

questions.question: What are JavaScript (ES) modules, and what's the difference between named and default exports/imports?
questions.answer: ES modules let code be split into separate files that explicitly export and import functionality, avoiding global-namespace pollution. A module can have multiple named exports (export const foo = 1; export function bar() {}), each imported by its exact name with optional renaming: import { foo, bar as baz } from './module.js'. A module can additionally have one default export (export default function () {} or export default value), imported without braces and under any name the importer chooses: import myThing from './module.js'. Named exports are explicit, support many per module, are easier to tree-shake, and are more refactor-safe because tooling catches every import using the same name; a default export is convenient when a module's whole purpose is 'one main thing,' but because importers can name it anything, tooling can't enforce naming consistency across a codebase the way it can with named exports - which is why many style guides now favor named exports for library and internal code.

What are Symbols in JavaScript, and what are they typically used for?
questions.answer: Symbol is a primitive type introduced in ES6 whose defining property is uniqueness - every call to Symbol('description') creates a brand-new, guaranteed-unique value, even if two symbols share the same description string, and symbols are never implicitly coerced to strings, avoiding accidental key collisions. The main practical use is as an object property key that won't clash with string keys or with keys added by other code or libraries, e.g., attaching metadata to an object without risking overwriting an existing property. The language itself uses 'well-known symbols' for exactly this purpose, customizing built-in behavior without touching regular property names - Symbol.iterator (defines for...of/spread behavior), Symbol.asyncIterator, Symbol.hasInstance (customizes instanceof), and Symbol.toPrimitive (customizes coercion), among others. Symbols are also non-enumerable by default in for...in, Object.keys(), and JSON.stringify(), making them suitable for framework-internal properties that shouldn't show up in ordinary iteration. Symbol.for(key) additionally creates or retrieves symbols from a global registry, allowing intentional sharing of a symbol across code by key.

questions.question: What is the difference between Map/Set and plain objects/arrays, and when would you reach for a WeakMap or WeakSet?
questions.answer: Map and Set are dedicated keyed-collection types from ES6. Map stores key-value pairs with keys of any type (including objects and NaN - unlike plain objects, which coerce all keys to strings), preserves insertion order, exposes a direct .size, and is generally faster for frequent additions/removals than a plain object used as a map. Set stores unique values of any type, useful for deduplication ([...new Set(array)]) and membership testing. Plain objects/arrays remain preferable for JSON-serializability, literal syntax, or object methods. WeakMap and WeakSet are restricted variants whose keys (WeakMap) or values (WeakSet) must be objects (or non-registered symbols for WeakMap keys) and are held weakly - an entry doesn't prevent its key/value from being garbage-collected if nothing else references it, and once collected, the entry disappears too. Because of this they're deliberately non-iterable and have no .size, and are ideal for attaching metadata to objects (e.g., caching computed data per DOM node) without keeping those objects alive forever.

questions.question: What is the difference between event bubbling and event capturing in the DOM?
questions.answer: When a DOM event fires, it propagates through the tree in up to three phases: capturing (the event travels from the document root down toward the target, notifying ancestors first), target (the event reaches the actual element it occurred on), and bubbling (the event then travels back up from the target through each ancestor to the root). By default, addEventListener(type, handler) registers the handler for the bubbling phase; passing true (or { capture: true }) as the third argument registers it for the capturing phase instead. Both phases exist for historical reasons - early browsers implemented only one or the other (Netscape favored capturing, Internet Explorer favored bubbling), and the W3C standard settled on supporting both. In practice, almost all code relies on the default bubbling phase, since that's what makes event delegation possible; capturing is used rarely, mainly to intercept an event before it reaches a target that might call stopPropagation() and prevent an ancestor's bubbling handler from ever running.

questions.question: What is strict mode ("use strict"), and what behavior changes does it introduce?
questions.answer: 'use strict' opts a script, module, function, or class body into a restricted variant of JavaScript with different (not just more strictly checked) semantics, aimed at eliminating silent failures and unsafe patterns. Concretely, strict mode turns previously-silent mistakes into thrown errors: assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of silently creating a global, and assigning to a non-writable property (like a frozen object's property, or the global NaN) throws a TypeError instead of doing nothing. It changes this in a plain function call from the global object to undefined. It disallows the with statement and duplicate function parameter names, and it makes optimizations easier for engines because behavior becomes more predictable. ES modules and class bodies are automatically in strict mode, so 'use strict' is now largely a legacy concern for plain <script> tags or CommonJS files - but understanding its behavioral differences, especially the this change and the silent-failure-becomes-thrown-error theme, remains a common interview check on how well someone understands sloppy-mode JavaScript's quirks in the first place.

questions.question: What is garbage collection in JavaScript, and how can closures or detached DOM references lead to memory leaks despite it?
questions.answer: JavaScript manages memory automatically: it allocates memory when values are created and periodically reclaims memory for values no longer reachable from the program, without requiring manual free()-style calls. All modern engines implement this with a mark-and-sweep algorithm: starting from a set of roots (global variables and local variables of currently executing functions), the collector marks every object reachable by following references from those roots, then sweeps away everything left unmarked. This improves on the older reference-counting approach, which fails on circular references - two objects referencing each other but unreachable from any root would never hit zero references under counting, but mark-and-sweep correctly identifies such cycles as garbage since they're unreachable from the roots. Despite this, real leaks still happen: forgotten setInterval/setTimeout timers keep their closures (and everything those closures reference) alive indefinitely; event listeners left attached to elements that are otherwise removed from the DOM keep both the listener's closure and the detached element reachable; and accidental global variables (which strict mode helps prevent) live for the entire page lifetime. WeakMap/WeakSet exist specifically so code can reference objects without those references counting toward reachability, letting entries be collected once nothing else needs them.

questions.question: What causes an unbounded bundle size in a growing React app, and what tools/techniques would you use to diagnose and reduce it?
questions.answer: Common causes: importing entire libraries when only a small piece is used (e.g., importing all of Lodash instead of a single function), accidentally bundling server-only or dev-only code into the client bundle, duplicate versions of the same dependency pulled in by different packages, large third-party libraries (heavy chart/date libraries, moment.js instead of a lighter alternative) chosen without checking their size cost, and simply not code-splitting - shipping every route/feature in a single bundle instead of loading it on demand. To diagnose: use a bundle analyzer (`source-map-explorer`, `webpack-bundle-analyzer`, or Vite's `rollup-plugin-visualizer`) to see a treemap of what's actually contributing to bundle size, and check whether tree-shaking is actually working (some libraries aren't ESM-friendly and pull in more than expected). Fixes include route-level and component-level code splitting with `React.lazy`/dynamic `import()`, swapping heavy dependencies for lighter alternatives, ensuring imports are granular (`import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` rather than `import _ from 'lodash'`, or using a tree-shakeable package), and auditing for duplicate dependency versions via the bundler's dependency graph output.

questions.question: What's the difference between debouncing and throttling, and which would you use for a scroll handler versus a search input?
questions.answer: Debouncing delays execution until a burst of events stops - each new event resets the timer, so the function only runs once, after the last event in a rapid sequence, following a pause of the configured delay. Throttling instead guarantees the function runs at most once per fixed interval, regardless of how many events fire in between - it doesn't wait for things to stop, it just rate-limits how often the handler executes during continuous activity. A search-as-you-type input is the classic debounce use case: you don't want to fire an API call on every keystroke, only once the user pauses typing, since intermediate partial queries are wasted work. A scroll or resize handler (e.g., updating a 'sticky header is visible' state, or lazy-loading images as you scroll) is a better fit for throttling, since you generally want periodic updates during continuous scrolling, not just a single update after the user stops scrolling entirely - throttling every 100-200ms keeps the UI reasonably responsive to ongoing movement without running expensive work on every single scroll event (which can fire dozens of times per second).

questions.question: What is database denormalization, and when might you deliberately introduce redundancy into a schema?
questions.answer: Denormalization is the deliberate process of combining normalized tables or duplicating data to reduce the number of joins a query needs, trading storage space and write-complexity for faster reads. Where normalization organizes data to eliminate redundancy and prevent update anomalies, denormalization intentionally reintroduces some redundancy because, in read-heavy systems, the cost of repeatedly joining many normalized tables can outweigh the storage and write-consistency costs. Common scenarios where denormalization makes sense: (1) reporting/analytics (OLAP) workloads, where queries aggregate across huge volumes of data and joining a fully normalized star/snowflake schema repeatedly is expensive - pre-joining or pre-aggregating into wider, flatter tables speeds up dashboards significantly; (2) caching computed/aggregated values (e.g., storing a denormalized 'order_total' column on the Orders table instead of recalculating it from OrderLines every time it's read); (3) high-read, low-write systems where the performance gain from avoiding joins on every read clearly outweighs the extra work needed to keep duplicated data in sync on writes. The trade-off to always mention in an interview: denormalization increases the risk of data inconsistency (the same fact stored in multiple places can drift out of sync unless carefully maintained via triggers, application logic, or materialized views), and it should generally be a deliberate, measured optimization applied after profiling - not a default starting design.

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal partitioning and sharding, and what problems does each solve at scale?
questions.answer: Horizontal partitioning splits the rows of a single logical table into multiple smaller physical partitions, but all partitions still live within the same database instance - the database engine handles routing queries to the correct partition(s) transparently (often via partition pruning based on a WHERE clause matching the partition key, e.g., partitioning an orders table by year). It solves problems of query performance and maintainability on very large tables: queries that filter on the partition key only need to scan the relevant partition(s) instead of the whole table, and maintenance tasks (e.g., dropping old data by simply dropping a whole partition, or rebuilding indexes) become cheaper because they operate on smaller units. Vertical partitioning, by contrast, splits a table's columns rather than its rows - separating rarely-used or large columns (e.g., long text/blob fields) into a separate table to keep the frequently-accessed 'hot' columns compact and fast to scan. Sharding is a related but distinct, more aggressive technique: it splits data across multiple independent database instances/servers entirely, not just multiple partitions within one instance - each shard typically holds a distinct subset of rows (e.g., by customer region or a hash of the customer ID) and runs as its own separate database. Sharding solves a different class of problem: horizontal scaling beyond what a single machine's CPU/memory/disk/IOPS can handle, by distributing both storage and query load across many machines. The trade-off with sharding is significant added complexity - cross-shard queries/joins become expensive or require application-level aggregation, transactions spanning multiple shards lose easy ACID guarantees (typically requiring distributed transaction protocols or eventual consistency), and resharding (rebalancing data as growth patterns change) is a nontrivial operational challenge. In short: reach for partitioning first to improve performance/manageability within a single database; reach for sharding only when you've genuinely outgrown what a single database server can handle, since it's a heavier architectural commitment.

What's the difference between solving a problem recursively vs. iteratively, and what happens if a recursive function is missing a proper base case?
questions.answer:
An iterative solution uses a loop and mutable state to repeat steps until a condition is met, using constant stack space regardless of how many repetitions occur. A recursive solution has a function call itself with a smaller version of the problem, relying on the call stack to hold the state of each pending call; it often reads closer to the problem's mathematical definition (e.g., factorial, tree traversal) and can be more concise, at the cost of the memory and (usually) time overhead of maintaining stack frames.

A recursive function needs a base case - a condition where it stops calling itself and returns a value directly - for the recursion to terminate. Without one (or if the recursive step never actually converges toward the base case, e.g. a typo passing n instead of n - 1), every call pushes another frame onto the call stack indefinitely. Because JavaScript engines generally don't implement tail call optimization, this will eventually exhaust the stack and throw a RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, rather than looping forever. This is a common bug source and a common interview probe: tracing through a recursive function to check that every branch either hits a base case or makes genuine progress toward one.

questions.question: What is a polyfill, and how does it differ from what a transpiler like Babel does?
questions.answer:
A polyfill is runtime code that implements a missing feature so older environments behave as if they supported it natively - for example, a script that checks if Array.prototype.flat exists and, if not, defines an equivalent implementation. Polyfills address missing APIs/built-ins: things you call at runtime (methods, global objects, Web APIs).

A transpiler like Babel instead addresses missing syntax: it's a build-time tool that rewrites newer JavaScript syntax the target environment can't parse at all (arrow functions, optional chaining, class fields, async/await) into equivalent older syntax the environment can run - this happens before the code ever executes, whereas a polyfill's fallback code runs inside the target environment itself. The two are complementary and usually used together: Babel transpiles new syntax down to something parseable by an older engine, while separately including polyfills (historically via core-js, often through @babel/preset-env's targeted 'useBuiltIns' config) for any new built-ins the transpiled code depends on but the target runtime doesn't provide, since transpilation alone can't invent a missing method that doesn't exist in the runtime.

questions.question: What is CORS, and why does a browser block certain cross-origin requests by default?
questions.answer:
By default, browsers enforce the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one origin (scheme + domain + port) cannot read the response of a request it makes to a different origin, unless that other origin explicitly opts in. This exists to stop a malicious site from silently using a visitor's authenticated session on another site (e.g., their bank) to read private data via a background fetch - the request itself may fire, but the browser withholds the response from the calling script unless authorized.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is the mechanism servers use to opt in to specific cross-origin access, via response headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For 'simple' requests (basic GET/POST with common headers), the browser sends the request as normal but only exposes the response to the calling script if the server's response includes the right CORS headers; for more complex requests (custom headers, non-simple methods like PUT/DELETE, certain content types), the browser first sends an automatic OPTIONS 'preflight' request to check the server permits it before sending the real request. Credentialed requests (cookies, Authorization headers) require the server to specify an exact allowed origin rather than a wildcard, plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, since allowing credentials with a wildcard origin would defeat the protection entirely.

questions.question: What's the difference between a repaint and a reflow in the browser's rendering pipeline, and why do transform/opacity animations perform better than animating top/left?
questions.answer:
The browser's rendering pipeline runs roughly: recalculate style → layout (reflow) → paint → composite. A reflow (layout) recalculates the geometry - position and size - of elements, and is triggered by changes that affect layout, like width, height, top/left with positioning, or adding/removing DOM nodes; because layout is often relational (one element's size affects its neighbors), a reflow can cascade and recompute large portions of the page. A repaint only redraws pixels - updating visual appearance without changing geometry - triggered by properties like color, background-color, or visibility; it's cheaper than reflow since it skips the geometry recalculation step, but still requires re-rasterizing pixels.

transform and opacity are cheapest of all: modern browsers can animate them on the compositor thread alone, skipping both layout and paint entirely - the GPU just repositions or fades an already-rasterized layer (texture) each frame, rather than recalculating layout or repainting on every frame. That's why translateX(100px) for a moving element is far smoother than animating its left property, which forces a full reflow on every animation frame, and why 'use transform/opacity for animations' is standard performance advice - it lets the animation stay off the main thread, avoiding jank from competing with the JavaScript that's also running there.

questions.question: What are sparse arrays (array "holes"), and how do they affect methods like forEach() and map() versus a plain for loop?
questions.answer:
A sparse array has 'holes' - indices within its length that were never assigned a value, as opposed to a dense array where every index up to length - 1 has one. Holes are distinct from explicit undefined values, even though reading a hole also returns undefined.

const sparse = [1, , 3]; // index 1 is a hole, not undefined
console.log(sparse.length); // 3
console.log(1 in sparse); // false - the index doesn't exist

Most iteration array methods - forEach(), map(), filter(), some(), every() - explicitly skip holes: their callback simply isn't invoked for indices that don't exist, though map() still preserves the hole's position in the result array (the resulting array is the same length, with the hole 'shifted through' unchanged). A plain for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) loop, by contrast, doesn't distinguish holes at all - it accesses every index including holes, returning undefined for each one and running the loop body regardless. for...in also skips holes (and inherited/non-enumerable properties), similarly to the array methods. Sort behavior is another quirk: sort() preserves holes but always moves them to the end of the array, after any explicit undefined values. Sparse arrays usually arise unintentionally (assigning to an out-of-bounds index, or using new Array(5)), and are generally best avoided since they behave inconsistently across different APIs.

questions.question: What is the arguments object, and how does it differ from using rest parameters (...args)?
questions.answer:
Inside any non-arrow function, arguments is an automatically-available, array-like object holding every argument the function was actually called with, regardless of how many parameters were formally declared. It's array-like (has a length and numeric indices) but is not a true array - it lacks methods like map(), filter(), or forEach() directly (they must be borrowed via Array.prototype.map.call(arguments, ...) or converted first with Array.from(arguments) or [...arguments]).

Rest parameters (function f(...args) {}) collect the extra arguments into a genuine Array, immediately usable with all array methods, and - unlike arguments - can be combined with named parameters to capture only the 'remaining' args after the named ones (function f(first, ...rest) {}), whereas arguments always contains every argument regardless of named parameters. arguments also has quirky legacy behavior in non-strict mode (its values can stay linked to the named parameters, so reassigning one can affect the other) that rest parameters don't share. Critically, arrow functions have no arguments object of their own at all - inside an arrow function, arguments refers to the enclosing non-arrow function's arguments (or throws if there isn't one), which is one of several reasons rest parameters are now the preferred, unambiguous way to access a function's arguments.

questions.question: How do getters and setters work on JavaScript objects and classes, and when would you reach for them?
What does Object.defineProperty() do, and what do the writable, enumerable, and configurable descriptors control?
What do the replacer and space arguments of JSON.stringify() do, and how would you handle circular references when serializing an object?
questions.answer:
JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space) accepts two optional arguments beyond the value to serialize. replacer either is a function called for every key/value pair during serialization - returning a Number/String/Boolean/null keeps that transformed value, returning undefined/a Function/Symbol omits the property, and returning anything else recurses into it - letting you filter out sensitive fields or transform values (e.g., converting a Date to a custom string); or it can be an array of key names, in which case only those keys are included in the output. space controls formatting for readability: a number of spaces (capped at 10) or a literal string used for indentation at each nesting level - omitted or 0 produces compact, single-line JSON.

JSON.stringify(user, ['name', 'email'], 2); // only these two keys, pretty-printed

JSON.stringify() throws a TypeError ('cyclic object value') if the object contains a circular reference, since JSON itself has no way to represent one. To handle it, either write a replacer function that tracks already-visited objects (e.g., with a WeakSet) and replaces repeat references with a placeholder like '[Circular]', use a library designed for this (e.g., Douglas Crockford's cycle.js), or, if the goal is actually cloning rather than serializing to a string, use structuredClone(), which supports circular references natively.

questions.question: What is structuredClone(), and how does it differ from cloning with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())?
questions.answer:
structuredClone() is a built-in global function that performs a deep clone of a value using the structured clone algorithm - the same underlying algorithm browsers use internally for postMessage() and IndexedDB. It correctly handles cases the JSON round-trip approach cannot: it supports circular references (an object referencing itself, directly or indirectly) without throwing; it correctly clones Date objects, Map, Set, RegExp, and typed arrays/ArrayBuffer as their proper types, rather than mangling or dropping them; and it preserves undefined values in objects rather than omitting them.

const original = { date: new Date(), map: new Map([['a', 1]]) };
original.self = original; // circular reference
const clone = structuredClone(original); // works fine

What structuredClone() cannot clone (it throws a DataCloneError): functions, DOM nodes, and a few other non-serializable types like Error objects with custom prototypes and Symbol-keyed properties - JSON.stringify() silently drops functions and undefined instead of throwing, which can mask bugs. Overall, structuredClone() is strictly more robust and is now the recommended default for deep-cloning in modern JavaScript, with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) mainly persisting in codebases for legacy or environment-compatibility reasons.

questions.question: What is BigInt, and what problem does it solve that regular JavaScript numbers can't?
questions.answer:
Regular JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 double-precision floats, which can only represent integers exactly up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1); beyond that, integer arithmetic silently loses precision (e.g., 9007199254740993 === 9007199254740992 evaluates to true, because both round to the same floating-point value). BigInt is a separate primitive type, added in ES2020, that represents arbitrary-precision integers of any size, limited only by available memory, with exact arithmetic and no rounding error.

const big = 9007199254740993n; // trailing 'n' makes it a BigInt literal
typeof big; // 'bigint'
big + 1n; // 9007199254740994n - exact, no precision loss

BigInt solves problems like working with 64-bit integer IDs from databases or external systems, cryptographic computations requiring exact large-integer math, and any domain (e.g., financial systems dealing with very large exact values) where precision beyond 2^53 matters. The trade-off: BigInt and Number are separate types that can't be mixed directly in arithmetic (1n + 1 throws a TypeError - one side must be explicitly converted), and BigInt cannot be serialized by JSON.stringify() without a custom replacer, since JSON has no native bigint representation.

questions.question: What are TypedArrays and ArrayBuffer, and when would you use them instead of a regular array?
questions.answer:
An ArrayBuffer represents a fixed-length, raw chunk of binary memory with no inherent format - it can't be read or written directly. A TypedArray (Int8Array, Uint32Array, Float64Array, and similar) is a 'view' onto an ArrayBuffer that interprets its bytes as a specific numeric type, letting you read and write that memory using familiar array-index syntax while working with fixed-size, fixed-type binary data.

const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(8); // 8 raw bytes
const view = new Uint32Array(buffer); // interpret as two 32-bit unsigned ints
view[0] = 42;

Unlike a regular Array, which can hold mixed types and grow/shrink dynamically, a typed array has a fixed length set at creation and every element must be the same numeric type, with out-of-range values wrapped via modulo arithmetic rather than throwing. You'd reach for typed arrays instead of regular arrays when working with binary data directly - parsing a file format, processing audio/image/video data (e.g., via the Canvas or Web Audio APIs), handling data received from a WebSocket or WebGL buffer, or communicating with native code - because they offer predictable, compact memory layout and much better performance for large numeric datasets than an array of boxed Number objects. Multiple typed array views can also share the same underlying ArrayBuffer at different offsets, letting you interpret the same raw memory as different structured fields (e.g., parsing a binary protocol with mixed integer sizes).

questions.question: What are the differences between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies in terms of persistence, size limits, and accessibility from the server?
questions.answer:
localStorage persists indefinitely - data survives page reloads, tab closes, and browser restarts, until explicitly cleared by code or the user - and is scoped per origin, shared across every tab/window for that origin. sessionStorage behaves the same API-wise, but is scoped per tab: data is cleared when that specific tab or window closes, and separate tabs on the same site each get their own independent sessionStorage even if opened to the same URL. Neither localStorage nor sessionStorage is ever automatically sent to the server - they're purely client-side and only accessible via JavaScript.

Cookies work differently: they're automatically attached to every matching HTTP request the browser makes to the server (based on domain/path), making them the only one of the three natively readable by server-side code without any extra client logic, but they carry a much smaller size budget (~4KB per cookie, with a limit on the number of cookies per domain) versus the roughly 5 - 10MB typically available to localStorage/sessionStorage per origin. Cookies also support security-relevant attributes the Storage APIs lack entirely: HttpOnly (invisible to JavaScript), Secure (HTTPS-only transmission), and SameSite (controls cross-site sending, mitigating CSRF) - which is exactly why cookies, not localStorage, are the recommended choice for anything sensitive like session identifiers.

questions.question: What is immutability in JavaScript, and how do you enforce it for objects/arrays given that const alone doesn't make a value immutable?
questions.answer:
Immutability means a value, once created, cannot be changed in place - any 'modification' instead produces a new value, leaving the original untouched. const only prevents reassigning the variable binding itself; it does nothing to the value it points to, so a const object or array can still have its properties mutated freely (const obj = { a: 1 }; obj.a = 2; is perfectly legal).

To actually enforce immutability: Object.freeze(obj) prevents adding, removing, or reassigning top-level properties (though it's shallow - nested objects inside a frozen object remain fully mutable unless recursively frozen too); for arrays and objects generally, following an 'always copy, never mutate' discipline using non-mutating operations - the spread operator ({...obj, key: newValue}, [...arr, newItem]), Array methods that return new arrays (map, filter, concat, toSorted, toSpliced) instead of their mutating counterparts (push, sort, splice) - achieves the same effect at the code-pattern level without relying on freeze(). For deeply nested structures, dedicated immutable-data libraries (Immutable.js, or Immer, which lets you write code that looks mutating but produces a new immutable value under the hood) are common in practice, especially in state-management contexts (Redux) where immutability is required so change detection can rely on cheap reference-equality checks rather than expensive deep comparisons.

questions.question: What are WeakMap/WeakSet used for, and why can't you iterate over their entries directly?
questions.answer:
WeakMap and WeakSet hold their keys (WeakMap) or values (WeakSet) weakly - meaning that reference doesn't count toward keeping the object alive for garbage collection. If nothing else in the program references an object that's used as a WeakMap key or WeakSet value, the garbage collector is free to reclaim it, and its corresponding WeakMap/WeakSet entry disappears along with it automatically. This makes them well-suited for attaching metadata or caching data associated with objects - like per-DOM-node state, or memoization caches keyed by object identity - without that association itself preventing the object from ever being cleaned up (which would be a memory leak if a regular Map were used instead).

They deliberately have no way to list their contents - no keys(), values(), entries(), forEach(), size, or support for for...of - and this restriction exists specifically because of how they interact with garbage collection: exposing an enumerable list of current entries would mean that list's contents (and therefore observable program behavior) could change based on exactly when the garbage collector happens to run, which is inherently non-deterministic and not something the language can guarantee or expose safely. If you need to enumerate what's stored, a regular Map or Set is the right choice; WeakMap/WeakSet are for cases where you only ever need to look something up given a key you already have, never list everything that's currently stored.

questions.question: What's the difference between array-like objects (e.g., NodeList, arguments) and true arrays, and how do you convert one into a real array?
questions.answer:
An array-like object has indexed elements and a length property - enough structure to loop over with a plain for loop - but doesn't inherit from Array.prototype, so it lacks array methods like map(), filter(), reduce(), and forEach() (some, like NodeList, do have their own forEach, but not the full array method set). Common examples: the arguments object inside a function, a DOM NodeList returned by querySelectorAll(), an HTMLCollection returned by getElementsByClassName(), and strings (indexable and have length, but are also immutable, unlike real arrays).

Two standard ways to convert an array-like object into a genuine Array: Array.from(arrayLike) (also accepts an optional mapping function as a second argument, combining conversion and transformation in one call), or the spread operator, [...arrayLike] - which only works if the array-like object is also iterable (has Symbol.iterator, as NodeList and arguments both do, but a plain custom { length: 3, 0: 'a', ... } object without an iterator would not work with spread, only with Array.from()).

const nodes = document.querySelectorAll('div');
Array.from(nodes).map(el => el.textContent); // now has full array methods

Once converted, all standard array methods become available, which is why this conversion is a common first step before doing any non-trivial processing of DOM query results or a function's arguments.

questions.question: In a JavaScript project, what's the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests, and what's the difference between a mock and a stub?
questions.answer:
A unit test verifies a single piece of code (a function, a class, a module) in isolation, with all its dependencies replaced by test doubles, so a failure points precisely at the unit under test rather than something it depends on - these run fastest and are cheapest to write and maintain. An integration test verifies that multiple real units (or a unit plus a real dependency, like an actual database or API) work correctly together, catching issues at the boundaries between components that isolated unit tests, by design, can't see. An end-to-end (E2E) test drives the whole system as a real user would - typically through an actual browser (via tools like Playwright or Cypress) - exercising the full stack including UI, network, and backend; these are the slowest and most brittle but give the highest confidence that the system genuinely works as a whole.

A stub is a simple test double that returns fixed, predetermined values when called, used to isolate the code under test from a real dependency without caring how or whether the stub itself is called - it's for controlling state so the test has predictable inputs to work with. A mock goes further: it's a test double that also records and lets you verify interactions - was this function called, how many times, and with what arguments - turning the test double itself into part of the assertion (e.g., 'verify the payment API was called exactly once with these parameters'), rather than just supplying canned data. The rule of thumb: use a stub when you're testing state/output, and a mock when you're testing behavior/interaction.

questions.question: How would you go about debugging a memory leak in a running JavaScript application, and what tools would you use?
questions.answer:
The standard approach uses Chrome DevTools' Memory panel to take heap snapshots at different points in time - for example, before and after repeating an action (like opening and closing a modal, or navigating between pages) several times - and comparing them. If memory keeps climbing after an action that should be memory-neutral, that's a strong signal of a leak. The Memory panel's 'Comparison' view between two snapshots highlights which object types grew, and the 'Retainers' view for a specific object shows exactly what's still referencing it, which is usually the fastest way to trace a leak back to its source (an uncleared timer, a lingering event listener, a growing cache/array, or a closure holding onto more than it needs).

A specific and very common pattern to look for is detached DOM nodes: elements removed from the visible page (e.g., via innerHTML = '' or removeChild()) but still referenced by a JavaScript variable, closure, or forgotten event listener - the garbage collector can't reclaim them because something still holds a reference, even though they're no longer part of the visible document. DevTools' heap snapshot flags these directly as 'Detached DOM tree' entries. Beyond heap snapshots, the Performance panel's memory timeline (a sawtooth pattern indicates normal allocation/GC cycles; a steadily rising baseline between GC cycles indicates a leak), and the 'Allocation instrumentation on timeline' recording mode (which tracks exactly where each allocation happened) round out the standard workflow for isolating the leaking code path.

questions.question: What's the difference between Array.prototype.slice() and Array.prototype.splice(), and which one mutates the original array?
questions.answer:
slice(start, end) returns a shallow copy of a portion of the array from start up to (but not including) end, as a brand-new array - the original array is completely untouched. splice(start, deleteCount, ...itemsToInsert) instead changes the original array in place: it removes deleteCount elements starting at start, optionally inserts new elements at that position, and returns an array of the elements that were removed - it mutates the array it's called on and does not return a copy of the whole array.

const arr = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'];
arr.slice(1, 3); // ['b', 'c'] - new array; arr is unchanged
arr.splice(1, 2, 'X'); // ['b', 'c'] - removed elements; arr is now ['a', 'X', 'd', 'e']

A simple mnemonic: splice has the extra 'p', standing for the extra power it has to permanently alter the original array; slice only takes a read-only snapshot. Because splice mutates, it's the tool for actually removing or inserting elements in place (e.g., removing an item from a list by index), while slice is the tool when you need an unmodified copy of a sub-range - including as a common trick to non-destructively clone an entire array (arr.slice()) before calling a mutating method on the copy instead of the original.

What is tail call optimization (TCO), and why can't you reliably depend on it across JavaScript engines today?
questions.answer:
A tail call is a function call made as the very last action of another function, with its result returned directly (return otherFn()). Tail call optimization reuses the current function's stack frame for that call instead of pushing a new one, so a properly tail-recursive function can recurse indefinitely without growing the call stack or risking a stack overflow. ES2015 (ES6) formally specified this behavior - called Proper Tail Calls (PTC) - as a required part of the language.

In practice, only Safari's JavaScriptCore engine implements PTC as specified. V8 (Chrome, Node.js) briefly shipped an experimental implementation but removed it, and Mozilla's SpiderMonkey (Firefox) never implemented it; both cited debugging difficulties (stack traces losing information when frames are elided) and real-world performance regressions as reasons. Because the two most widely-used engines don't support it, and there's no indication that will change, JavaScript code intended to run across environments cannot rely on TCO to avoid stack overflows in deep recursion - the practical workaround is to rewrite deeply recursive algorithms iteratively, or use an explicit trampoline pattern that manually manages the 'recursive' calls in a loop.

questions.question: What's the difference between the CommonJS module system (require/module.exports) and native ES Modules (import/export)?
questions.answer: CommonJS (Node.js's original module system) loads modules synchronously: require() blocks until the target file has fully executed and returns its module.exports object, and require() calls can appear anywhere in code, including conditionally inside an if block. ES Modules use import/export, are resolved and loaded asynchronously (or synchronously in a well-defined order in Node.js, but conceptually async for the browser), and static import/export declarations must appear at the top level of a module - they're hoisted and resolved before any module code runs, which is what enables tooling to statically analyze the dependency graph. That static structure is the key practical advantage of ESM: bundlers can determine exactly what's imported and exported without running any code, enabling tree shaking (dead-code elimination) - something CommonJS's dynamic require() calls fundamentally can't support, since what a module exports can depend on runtime logic. ESM also runs in strict mode automatically, supports top-level await, and is natively supported by modern browsers without bundling, whereas CommonJS requires a bundler for browser use. Node.js supports both today, but mixing them in one project can cause interoperability friction (e.g., a CommonJS package's default export shape when imported from ESM).

questions.question: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), and what JavaScript/DOM practices help prevent it?
questions.answer:
Cross-Site Scripting is a vulnerability where an attacker gets their own JavaScript to execute in another user's browser within your site's origin - typically by injecting a script through unsanitized user input that later gets rendered as live HTML/JS rather than as inert text. Once that script runs, it has the same access as your site's legitimate code: it can read cookies (unless HttpOnly), make authenticated requests, or exfiltrate data from localStorage.

Key prevention practices: never insert untrusted data into the DOM via innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, or template literals injected as raw HTML - use textContent, or a framework's built-in escaping (React/Vue auto-escape interpolated text by default) which only bypasses escaping through an explicit, clearly-named opt-in like dangerouslySetInnerHTML or v-html; treat any use of that opt-in as a place requiring careful sanitization (e.g., with DOMPurify) of the exact HTML being inserted; avoid eval(), new Function(), and passing strings to setTimeout/setInterval, since these execute arbitrary code; and set a Content-Security-Policy header restricting which script sources can execute, as a defense-in-depth layer even if an injection slips through application code. XSS remains one of OWASP's top web vulnerability categories precisely because a single unescaped output point is enough to compromise a page.

questions.question: Why is storing authentication tokens in localStorage risky, and what's a safer alternative?
questions.answer:
localStorage is fully readable by any JavaScript running on the page, with no built-in protection mechanism. If an attacker manages to run any script in your origin via XSS - through a vulnerable dependency, an unescaped user input field, or a compromised third-party script - that script can call localStorage.getItem('token') and send the value to an attacker-controlled server in a single line, with no browser warning and no way for the app to prevent it. Because the token is unbounded in time (it stays valid until it's revoked or expires), a single successful XSS exploit can result in an indefinitely reusable stolen credential, not just abuse limited to the current tab session.

OWASP's guidance is explicit: do not store session identifiers in local storage, since the data is always accessible by JavaScript; cookies can mitigate this specific risk via the HttpOnly flag, which makes the cookie's value completely invisible to any JavaScript, including an attacker's injected script - the browser attaches HttpOnly cookies to requests automatically, but no script can read or exfiltrate the token itself. The trade-off is that cookie-based auth introduces CSRF risk instead, since cookies are attached automatically to cross-site requests too, which is mitigated with the SameSite cookie attribute and/or anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing requests. A common production pattern is to keep a short-lived access token only in memory (a JS variable, not any persistent storage) and store a longer-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly, SameSite cookie.

questions.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism, and which (if either) does JavaScript actually support?
questions.answer:
Concurrency means structuring a program to make progress on multiple tasks over overlapping time periods, without necessarily executing them at the exact same instant - tasks are interleaved, taking turns, sharing a single execution resource. Parallelism means literally executing multiple tasks at the same physical instant, which requires multiple actual processing units (cores) running simultaneously.

JavaScript's core execution model - a single thread driven by an event loop - is concurrent, not parallel: async operations (Promises, setTimeout, event callbacks) don't run 'at the same time' as your synchronous code; they're queued and interleaved onto the same single thread whenever it becomes free, giving the appearance of doing multiple things at once without ever truly running two pieces of JS simultaneously. True parallelism is available, but only by explicitly spinning up separate threads via Web Workers (browser) or worker_threads (Node.js) - each worker runs on its own OS thread and can execute JavaScript literally simultaneously with the main thread, communicating only via message passing since they don't share memory by default (aside from opt-in SharedArrayBuffer). So: JavaScript's everyday async model is concurrency; genuine parallelism requires explicitly opting into workers.
