questions.question: What does [10, 1, 2].sort() output by default, and why? How do you correctly sort an array of numbers?
questions.answer:
[10, 1, 2].sort() outputs [1, 10, 2]. By default, sort() converts every element to a string and compares them lexicographically by their UTF-16 code unit values, rather than numerically - so '10' sorts before '2' because the character '1' has a lower code unit value than '2', the same way 'apple' sorts before 'banana'. This trips up anyone expecting numeric ordering by default.

To sort numbers correctly, pass an explicit compare function: (a, b) => a - b for ascending, or (a, b) => b - a for descending.

[10, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 10]

The compare function should return a negative number if a should come before b, a positive number if b should come before a, and 0 if they're equivalent; subtracting satisfies this cleanly for numbers. Note that sort() also mutates the array in place and returns the same reference (not a new array) - if the original order needs to be preserved, sort a copy first (e.g., [...arr].sort(...) or, in newer environments, the non-mutating toSorted() method).

questions.question: What are private class fields (#field), and how do they differ from a conventionally "private" property named with a leading underscore?
What happens internally, step by step, when you call a function with the new keyword?
questions.answer:
When new Foo(...args) is executed, four things happen in order: (1) a brand-new, empty object is created, with its internal [[Prototype]] set to Foo.prototype (so it inherits everything defined there); (2) the constructor function Foo is invoked with this bound to that new object, and the given arguments passed in; (3) the constructor's body runs, typically assigning properties onto this; and (4) if the constructor explicitly returns an object, that returned object becomes the result of the whole new expression instead of the object created in step 1 - but if it returns nothing, or returns a primitive value (string, number, etc.), the originally-created object (with the properties set on it) is used as the result instead, and the returned primitive is discarded.

function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
const p = new Point(1, 2); // p.x === 1, p instanceof Point === true

Classes behave the same way underneath but add a guardrail: attempting to call a class without new throws a TypeError, since classes can only be instantiated via new - a deliberate restriction not shared by ordinary constructor functions, which can technically be called without new (just with unintended this binding, usually pointing at the global object or undefined in strict mode).

questions.question: What is a tagged template literal, and what's a practical use case for one?
What's the difference between RegExp.prototype.exec(), test(), and String.prototype.match(), and what's the classic lastIndex gotcha with the global (g) flag?
questions.answer:
test(str) returns a boolean - whether the pattern matches anywhere in the string - and is the simplest choice when you only need a yes/no answer. exec(str) returns either null or a detailed match array (the full match, capture groups, index, and input string) for a single match, and is the underlying method that most other regex-related string methods call internally. match(regex) is a String method (not a RegExp method): without the g flag it behaves like exec() called once, returning the same detailed array; with the g flag it instead returns a simple array of all matched substrings (no capture group or index detail) since it needs to represent every match, not just one.

The lastIndex gotcha: a regex object with the g (or y, sticky) flag maintains internal state - a lastIndex property tracking where the next match search should resume - shared across successive calls to exec() or test() on the same regex object. This means calling test() or exec() repeatedly on the same global-flagged regex without resetting lastIndex can silently skip matches, or unexpectedly return false/null on a string that does contain a match, because the search resumes from wherever the last call left off rather than from the start.

const re = /foo/g;
re.test('foo foo'); // true, lastIndex now 3
re.test('foo foo'); // true, lastIndex now 7
re.test('foo foo'); // false! lastIndex was 7, nothing left to match

The fix is to either reset re.lastIndex = 0 before reuse, avoid the g flag when you only need a single test, or create a fresh regex literal per use rather than reusing a stored global-flagged one.
